shared_context.topic: difference between canker sore and herpes

atoms.1: To distinguish between a canker sore (aphthous stomatitis) and herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, several clinical features can be considered.
atoms.2: Aphthous stomatitis is also known as a canker sore.
atoms.3: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) is an infection.
atoms.4: Aphthous stomatitis typically occurs on non-keratinized mucosal surfaces.
atoms.5: Non-keratinized mucosal surfaces include the inside of the lips, cheeks, the floor of the mouth, and the soft palate.
atoms.6: Herpes simplex virus often affects keratinized mucosal surfaces.
atoms.7: Keratinized mucosal surfaces include the gingiva (gums), the hard palate, and the lips (herpes labialis).
atoms.8: Aphthous stomatitis presents as a round or oval ulcer with a yellow or white center and a red border.
atoms.9: Herpes simplex virus begins as grouped vesicles that rupture to form painful ulcers.
atoms.10: Herpes simplex virus lesions may crust over if on the lips.
atoms.11: Aphthous stomatitis is often recurrent without a clear trigger.
atoms.12: Stress, trauma, and certain foods can exacerbate aphthous stomatitis.
atoms.13: Herpes simplex virus recurrences are often triggered by factors such as fever, stress, sunlight, or immunosuppression.
atoms.14: Aphthous stomatitis typically does not have prodromal symptoms.
atoms.15: Herpes simplex virus is often preceded by prodromal symptoms such as tingling, itching, or pain in the area before the appearance of lesions.
atoms.17: Aphthous stomatitis ulcers last from 7 to 14 days and heal without scarring.
atoms.19: Herpes simplex virus lesions heal over 2 to 4 weeks.
atoms.20: Recurrent herpes simplex virus lesions tend to heal faster.
atoms.21: Aphthous stomatitis is usually not associated with systemic symptoms.
atoms.22: Primary herpes simplex virus infection may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy.

snippets.output: To distinguish between a canker sore (aphthous stomatitis) and herpes simplex virus (HSV) infection, several clinical features can be considered.
Aphthous stomatitis, also known as a canker sore, typically occurs on non-keratinized mucosal surfaces such as the inside of the lips, cheeks, the floor of the mouth, and the soft palate.
Herpes simplex virus (HSV) often affects keratinized mucosal surfaces, including the gingiva (gums), the hard palate, and the lips (herpes labialis).
Aphthous stomatitis presents as a round or oval ulcer with a yellow or white center and a red border.
Herpes simplex virus begins as grouped vesicles that rupture to form painful ulcers, and the lesions may crust over if on the lips.
Aphthous stomatitis is often recurrent without a clear trigger, although stress, trauma, and certain foods can exacerbate it.
Herpes simplex virus recurrences are often triggered by factors such as fever, stress, sunlight, or immunosuppression.
Aphthous stomatitis typically does not have prodromal symptoms.
Herpes simplex virus is often preceded by prodromal symptoms such as tingling, itching, or pain in the area before the appearance of lesions.
Aphthous stomatitis is painful, with ulcers lasting from 7 to 14 days and healing without scarring.
Herpes simplex virus is painful, with lesions healing over 2 to 4 weeks, and recurrent lesions tend to heal faster.
Aphthous stomatitis is usually not associated with systemic symptoms.
Primary herpes simplex virus infection may be accompanied by systemic symptoms such as fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy.
